subject: social
source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 1

questions.q: What percentage of Belgium’s population lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch?
questions.e: 59% Dutch (Flemish region), 40% French (Wallonia), 1% German.

questions.q: In Brussels, the capital of Belgium, the majority of people speak…
questions.e: In Brussels 80% speak French and 20% Dutch – the Dutch were a majority in the country but a minority in the capital.

questions.q: In which year was the Act passed that recognised Sinhala as the only official language of Sri Lanka?
questions.e: The 1956 Act disregarded Tamil – a major majoritarian measure.

questions.q: Sri Lanka became independent in…
questions.e: Sri Lanka emerged as an independent country in 1948.

questions.q: A belief that the majority community should rule a country in whichever way it wants, disregarding the wishes and needs of the minority, is called…
questions.e: Definition from the chapter: majoritarianism.

questions.q: Which religion did the new Sri Lankan constitution say the state shall protect and foster?
questions.e: Most Sinhala speakers are Buddhists; this measure increased Tamil alienation.

questions.q: Belgium amended its constitution four times between…
questions.e: Between 1970 and 1993 Belgium worked out its innovative power-sharing model.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of the Belgian model of power sharing?
questions.a: The majority Dutch community appoints all central ministers
w: Equal number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers in the central government
A community government elected by each language group
Brussels has a separate government with equal representation of both communities
questions.e: The constitution requires EQUAL numbers of Dutch and French-speaking ministers – no single community decides alone.

questions.q: The ‘community government’ in Belgium has powers regarding…
questions.e: It is elected by people of one language community – Dutch, French or German-speaking – wherever they live.

questions.q: What was the main result of majoritarian policies in Sri Lanka?
questions.a: Distrust grew into a civil war that ended in 2009
w: Tamil was made the only official language
Belgium-style community governments were set up
questions.e: Alienation of Sri Lankan Tamils led to demands for Tamil Eelam and a civil war.

questions.q: Which city was chosen as the headquarters of the European Union?
questions.e: Belgium’s successful accommodation made Brussels a fitting headquarters of the EU.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Belgian model helped avoid a possible division of the country on linguistic lines.
Reason (R): Belgian leaders recognised regional differences and cultural diversities and shared power among communities.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.e: Accommodation, not domination, kept Belgium united; R explains A.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sri Lanka adopted a series of majoritarian measures after independence.
Reason (R): The Sinhala-speaking community formed about 74 per cent of the population.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.e: Both are true, but being a majority does not explain why leaders chose majoritarianism – that was a political choice to secure dominance.

questions.q: Read the passage and answer: Why did the Sri Lankan Tamils feel alienated?
questions.a: Government policies denied them equal political rights and discriminated against them in jobs and opportunities
w: They were a majority in Colombo
The government gave them a separate state
questions.e: The passage lists the measures that made Tamils feel their interests were ignored.
questions.passage: In 1956, an Act was passed to recognise Sinhala as the only official language, thus disregarding Tamil. The governments followed preferential policies that favoured Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs. A new constitution stipulated that the state shall protect and foster Buddhism.

questions.q: Power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups. This is a…
questions.e: Prudential reasons stress better outcomes (stability, less conflict).

questions.q: ‘Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy.’ This is a…
questions.e: Moral reasons value the act of power sharing itself – people have a right to be consulted.

questions.q: The word ‘prudential’ means based on…
questions.a: careful calculation of gains and losses
questions.e: Prudential decisions are contrasted with decisions based purely on moral considerations.

questions.q: A legitimate government is one where…
questions.a: citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system
questions.e: This is the moral argument for power sharing.

questions.q: According to the chapter, the ‘tyranny of the majority’…
questions.a: is oppressive for the minority and often affects the majority adversely too
w: helps the majority in the long run
questions.e: Imposing the majority’s will looks attractive in the short run but undermines national unity.

questions.q: Which set of statements are arguments IN FAVOUR of power sharing? A. reduces conflict  B. decreases arbitrariness  C. delays decisions  D. accommodates diversities  E. increases instability  F. promotes participation
questions.e: C and E are arguments against it; the favourable ones are A, B, D, F (NCERT exercise 6).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Power sharing is good for democracy.
Reason (R): It helps to reduce the possibility of conflict between social groups.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.e: Both true; reducing conflict (a prudential reason) explains why it is good.

questions.q: Power shared among legislature, executive and judiciary is called…
questions.e: Organs at the same level exercise different powers – horizontal.

questions.q: Power shared among governments at different levels (Union, State, local) is called…
questions.e: Higher and lower levels of government – vertical.

questions.q: A system where each organ of government checks the others is called…
questions.e: E.g. judges are appointed by the executive but can check the executive and laws made by legislatures.

questions.q: A government formed by two or more parties together is called a…
questions.e: When parties form an alliance and win, they share power in a coalition.

questions.q: Reserved constituencies for weaker sections are an example of power sharing among…
questions.e: They give space to diverse social groups who might otherwise feel alienated.

questions.q: Interest groups of traders, farmers and industrial workers share power by…
questions.a: participating in governmental committees or influencing decision making
questions.e: This is power sharing through parties, pressure groups and movements.

questions.q: Match: 1. Organs of government 2. Different levels 3. Social groups 4. Two or more parties with A. Community government B. Separation of powers C. Coalition government D. Federal government
questions.e: Separation of powers, federal government, community government, coalition (NCERT exercise 8).

questions.q: In Lebanon’s power-sharing pact, the President must belong to the…
questions.e: PM – Sunni Muslim; Deputy PM – Orthodox Christian; Speaker – Shi’a Muslim (Khalil’s dilemma).

questions.q: Which community in Belgium was a minority in the country but a majority in Brussels?
questions.e: French speakers are 40% of Belgium but 80% of Brussels.
questions.passage: Belgium is a small country in Europe. Of its total population, 59 per cent lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch. Another 40 per cent lives in the Wallonia region and speaks French. The remaining one per cent speak German. In the capital city Brussels, 80 per cent speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking. The minority French-speaking community was relatively rich and powerful. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community who got the benefit of economic development and education much later.

questions.q: Why did the Dutch-speaking community resent the French-speaking community?
questions.a: The French-speakers were richer and more powerful; the Dutch got the benefits of development and education later
w: The Dutch were a minority in the country
The French-speakers wanted to join France
The Dutch were denied voting rights by the Constitution
questions.e: The passage says the minority French community was rich and powerful.
questions.passage: Belgium is a small country in Europe. Of its total population, 59 per cent lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch. Another 40 per cent lives in the Wallonia region and speaks French. The remaining one per cent speak German. In the capital city Brussels, 80 per cent speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking. The minority French-speaking community was relatively rich and powerful. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community who got the benefit of economic development and education much later.

questions.q: The ‘community government’ described in the passage is an example of power sharing among –
questions.e: It is elected by each language community, wherever its members live.
questions.passage: Between 1970 and 1993, Belgian leaders amended their constitution four times. Apart from the Central and the State Government, there is a third kind of government. This ‘community government’ is elected by people belonging to one language community – Dutch, French and German-speaking – no matter where they live. This government has the power regarding cultural, educational and language-related issues.

questions.q: Which subjects are handled by the community government of Belgium?
questions.e: Read the last line of the passage.
questions.passage: Between 1970 and 1993, Belgian leaders amended their constitution four times. Apart from the Central and the State Government, there is a third kind of government. This ‘community government’ is elected by people belonging to one language community – Dutch, French and German-speaking – no matter where they live. This government has the power regarding cultural, educational and language-related issues.

questions.q: Which statement about the Belgian model is NOT correct?
questions.a: The Dutch-speaking majority was given power to overrule the French-speaking minority
w: The number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government is equal
Brussels has a separate government with equal representation of both communities
State governments are not subordinate to the Central Government
questions.e: The Belgian constitution prescribes equality – no community can decide alone.

questions.q: Which was NOT a demand of the Sri Lankan Tamil parties?
questions.a: Making Sinhala the only official language
w: Recognition of Tamil as an official language
Equality of opportunity in education and jobs
questions.e: The 1956 Act making Sinhala the only official language was what Tamils opposed.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Belgian model helped to avoid civic strife and a division of the country on linguistic lines.
Reason (R): Belgian leaders recognised regional differences and cultural diversities and worked out arrangements to share power.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.e: Accommodation (R) produced peace and unity (A).

questions.q: Which situation best shows the PRUDENTIAL reason for power sharing?
questions.a: Sharing power reduced conflict between language groups in Belgium
w: People have a right to be consulted on how they are governed
Citizens must have a stake in the system
Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy
questions.e: Prudential = better outcomes (less conflict, stability); the others are moral reasons.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Majoritarianism can undermine the unity of a country.
Reason (R): In Sri Lanka, measures to establish Sinhala supremacy led to distrust and civil war.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.e: Sri Lanka is the textbook example of how majoritarian policies divide a country.

questions.q: What common lesson do the Belgium and Sri Lanka stories teach?
questions.a: Accommodating all groups keeps a country united, while majoritarianism can break it
w: Language should not be used in politics
questions.e: This is why power sharing is desirable.

questions.q: Why is horizontal power sharing called a system of ‘checks and balances’?
questions.a: Each organ checks the others, so no organ can exercise unlimited power
questions.e: Legislature, executive and judiciary keep each other in balance.

questions.q: Traders, industrialists, farmers and workers influence government decisions through their associations. This shows power sharing among…
questions.e: Interest groups share power by influencing decisions.

questions.q: Which is an example of vertical power sharing?
questions.a: Powers divided among Union, State and local governments
questions.e: Vertical = among levels of government.
